To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we designed a novel feedback-controlled anticoagulation system, in which the release of the anticoagulants heparin and hirudin from hydrogels is triggered by activated blood coagulant factors, and that this system can be used to tailor the anticoagulation response of biomaterial surfaces.

we designed and synthesized a new class of biohybrid materials that release heparin in a controlled fashion, triggered by different blood-clotting factors, which enables the formation of anticoagulant surfaces with improved efficiency.
heparin-containing biohybrid hydrogels with cleavable peptide linkers are promising candidates to provide a controlled release of anticoagulant molecules.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design and development of functional biohybrid materials, which are based on a modular approach.
the development of new biohybrid materials that combine the unique properties of biomacromolecules and synthetic polymers.
developing new biohybrid materials with adaptive release of bioactive molecules triggered by different blood components.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the presented biohybrid gels can be considered as a promising approach for the development of anticoagulant surfaces.
the release of heparine from the hydrogels was triggered by different blood clotting enzymes.
the release of heparine was triggered by the early blood coagulation factor FXa and kallikrein, which was shown to be more efficient than release triggered by thrombin.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the release of heparins from anticoagulation hydrogels can be controlled by different blood coaugulation factors and this release can be used to control the anticoagulation of biomaterials.
we have developed a new class of anticoagulant materials that are able to release heparin upon blood coagulation.
we have designed and synthesized a series of novel heparin-based biohybrid hydrogels with different cleavable peptide linkers.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the design of biohybrid materials for controlled drug delivery can be greatly enhanced by the introduction of molecular feedback mechanisms.
we have developed an anticoagulant surface that releases heparin in response to the first coagulation factors that are activated in the coagulation cascade.
the use of biomolecular circuits can be used to tailor the release of bioactive molecules from biomaterials to the specific needs of a given biomedical application.
